💡 Key Takeaways
  • LoRA adapters provide a great deal of customization for models of all shapes and sizes.
  • In this post, we take the Flux.1-Dev model for text-to-image generation because of its widespread popularity and adoption, and how to optimize its inference speed when using LoRAs (~2.3x).
  • Note that even though we demonstrate speedups with Flux, our belief is that our recipe is generic enough to be applied to other models as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LoRA adapters provide a great deal of customization for models of all shapes and sizes. When it comes to image generation, they can empower the models with different styles, different characters, and much more. Sometimes, they can also be leveraged to reduce inference latency. Hence, their importance is paramount, particularly when it comes to customizing and fine-tuning models.

In this post, we take the Flux.1-Dev model for text-to-image generation because of its widespread popularity and adoption, and how to optimize its inference speed when using LoRAs (~2.3x). It has over 30k adapters trained with it (as reported on the Hugging Face Hub platform). Therefore, its importance to the community is significant.

Note that even though we demonstrate speedups with Flux, our belief is that our recipe is generic enough to be applied to other models as well.

If you cannot wait to get started with the code, please check out the accompanying code repository.

It has been revealed that when serving LoRAs, it is common to hotswap (swap in and swap out different LoRAs) them. A LoRA changes the base model architecture. Additionally, LoRAs can be different from one another – each one of them could have varying ranks and different layers they target for adaptation. To account for these dynamic properties of LoRAs, we must take necessary steps to ensure the optimizations we apply are robust.

It has been revealed that for example, we can apply torch.compile on a model loaded with a particular LoRA to obtain speedups on inference latency. However, the moment we swap out the LoRA with a different one (with a potentially different configuration), we will run into recompilation issues, causing slowdowns in inference.

One can also fuse the LoRA parameters into the base model parameters, run compilation, and unfuse the LoRA parameters when loading newly introduced ones. However, this approach will again encounter the problem of recompilation whenever inference is run, due to potential architecture-level changes.

Recent findings suggest that our optimization recipe takes into account the above-mentioned situations to be as realistic as possible. Below are the key components of our optimization recipe:.

It has been revealed that note that amongst the above-mentioned, FP8 quantization is lossy but often provides the most formidable speed-memory trade-off. Even though we tested the recipe primarily using NVIDIA GPUs, it should work on AMD GPUs, too.

It has been revealed that in our previous blog posts (post 1 and post 2), we have already discussed the benefits of using the first three components of our optimization recipe. Applying them one by one is just a few lines of code:.

The FA3 processor comes from here.

The problems start surfacing when we try to swap in and swap out LoRAs into a compiled diffusion transformer (pipe.transformer) without triggering recompilation.

Recent findings suggest that normally, loading and unloading LoRAs will require recompilation, which defeats any speed advantage gained from compilation. Thankfully, there is a way to avoid the need for recompilation. By passing hotswap=True, diffusers will leave the model architecture unchanged and only exchange the weights of the LoRA adapter itself, which does not necessitate recompilation.

(As a reminder, the first call to pipe will be slow as torch.compile is a just-in-time compiler. However, the subsequent calls should be significantly faster.).

This generally allows for swapping LoRAs without recompilation, but there are limitations:.

For more information on hotswapping in Diffusers and its limitations, visit the hotswapping section of the documentation.

The benefits of this workflow become evident when we look at the inference latency without using compilation with hotswapping.

It has been revealed that the optimization recipe we have discussed so far assumes access to a powerful GPU like H100. However, what can we do when we’re limited to using consumer GPUs such as RTX 4090? Let’s find out.

Flux.1-Dev (without any LoRA), using the Bfloat16 data-type, takes ~33GB of memory to run. Depending on the size of the LoRA module, and without using any optimization, this memory footprint can increase even further. Many consumer GPUs like the RTX 4090 only have 24GB. Throughout the rest of this section, we will consider an RTX 4090 machine as our testbed.

First, to enable end-to-end execution of Flux.1-Dev, we can apply CPU offloading wherein components that are not needed to execute the current computation are offloaded to the CPU to free more accelerator memory. Doing so allows us to run the entire pipeline in ~22GB in 35.403 seconds on an RTX 4090. Enabling compilation can reduce the latency down to 31.205 seconds (1.12x speedup). In terms of code, it’s just a few lines:.

Notice that we didn’t apply the FP8 quantization here because it’s not supported with CPU offloading and compilation (supporting glitch thread). Therefore, just applying FP8 quantization to the Flux Transformer isn’t enough to mitigate the memory exhaustion problem, either. In this instance, we decided to remove it.

Therefore, to take advantage of the FP8 quantization scheme, we need to find a way to do it without CPU offloading. For Flux.1-Dev, if we additionally apply quantization to the T5 text encoder, we should be able to load and run the complete pipeline in 24GB. Below is a comparison of the results with and without the T5 text encoder being quantized (NF4 quantization from bitsandbytes).

As we can notice in the figure above, quantizing the T5 text encoder doesn’t incur too much of a quality loss. Combining the quantized T5 text encoder and FP8-quantized Flux Transformer with torch.compile gives us somewhat reasonable results – 9.668 seconds from 32.27 seconds (a massive ~3.3x speedup) without a noticeable quality drop.

It is possible to generate images with 24 GB of VRAM even without quantizing the T5 text encoder, but that would have made our generation pipeline slightly more complicated.

According to recent reports, we now have a way to run the entire Flux.1-Dev pipeline with FP8 quantization on an RTX 4090. We can apply the previously established optimization recipe for optimizing LoRA inference on the same hardware. Since FA3 isn’t supported on RTX 4090, we will stick to the following optimization recipe with T5 quantization newly added to the mix:.

In the table below, we show the inference latency numbers with different combinations of the above components applied.

To enable hotswapping without triggering recompilation, two hurdles have to be overcome. First, the LoRA scaling factor has to be converted into torch tensors from floats, which is achieved fairly easily. Second, the shape of the LoRA weights needs to padded to the largest required shape. That way, the data in the weights can be replaced without the need to reassign the whole attribute. This is why the max_rank argument discussed above is crucial. As we pad the values with zeros, the results remain unchanged, although the computation is slowed down a bit depending on how large the padding is.

Since no new LoRA attributes are added, this also requires that each LoRA after the first one can only target the same layers, or a subset of layers, that the first one targets. Thus, choose the order of loading wisely. If LoRAs target disjoint layers, there is the possibility to create a dummy LoRA that targets the union of all target layers.

To see the nitty-gritty of this implementation, visit the hotswap.py file in PEFT.

Recent findings suggest that this post outlined an optimization recipe for fast LoRA inference with Flux, demonstrating significant speedups. Our approach combines Flash Attention 3, torch.compile, and FP8 quantization while ensuring hotswapping capabilities without recompilation challenges. On high-end GPUs like the H100, this optimized setup provides a 2.23x speedup over the baseline.

According to recent reports, for consumer GPUs, specifically the RTX 4090, we tackled memory limitations by introducing T5 text encoder quantization (NF4) and leveraging regional compilation. This comprehensive recipe achieved a substantial 2.04x speedup, making LoRA inference on Flux viable and performant even with limited VRAM. The key insight is that by carefully managing compilation and quantization, the benefits of LoRA can be fully realized across different hardware configurations.

Hopefully, the recipes from this post will inspire you to optimize your LoRA-based use cases, benefitting from speedy inference.

Breaking: TimeScope: How Long Can Your Video Large Multimodal Model Go?

📅 23 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that timeScope is an open-source benchmark designed to measure how well vision-language models understand long videos.
  • It has been revealed that recent advances in multimodal AI have produced models claiming to understand hour-long videos.
  • Sources indicate that text benchmarks such as HELM and RULER have exposed the fragility of long-context claims, showing that models often struggle when tasks demand more than simple retrieval, like reasoning or aggregation at long context lengths.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that timeScope is an open-source benchmark designed to measure how well vision-language models understand long videos. By adding short “needle” clips into videos ranging from 1 minute to 8 hours, it evaluates three skills:.

It has been revealed that recent advances in multimodal AI have produced models claiming to understand hour-long videos. This trend mirrors progress in long-context language models, which excel at reasoning over lengthy text. Following this, vision-language systems now advertise context windows that can handle thousands of frames. But these claims require a closer look: do these models truly demonstrate understanding of the sequence of events? Are they limited to surface-level retrieval \ recognition? It's crucial to ask if their capabilities are being overstated.

Sources indicate that text benchmarks such as HELM and RULER have exposed the fragility of long-context claims, showing that models often struggle when tasks demand more than simple retrieval, like reasoning or aggregation at long context lengths. In the video domain, however, we're still playing catch-up. The most common test, Video Needle in a Haystack (VideoNIAH), injects static images as "needles" into videos, effectively measuring visual search rather than true temporal dynamics. As a result, even top-tier models advertising massive frame capacities are rarely trained beyond ~256 frames and see sharp drops on benchmarks like Video-MME when pushed further.

Sources indicate that this measurement gap leaves us wondering: What does it really mean for a model to "understand" long videos? To address this, we're excited to introduce TimeScope, a new open-source benchmark hosted on Hugging Face. TimeScope probes the limits of long-video capabilities by inserting several short (~5-10 second) video clips—our "needles"—into base videos ranging from 1 minute to 8 hours. With three distinct task types, it evaluates not just retrieval but synthesis, localization, and fine-grained motion analysis, providing a more holistic view of temporal comprehension.

The promise of long-video AI is transformative — enabling agents to summarize hours of footage, detect subtle anomalies, and answer complex questions about extended narratives. Integrated into robotics, these models could analyze prolonged operations, adapt in real time, and push autonomous decision-making. Just as powerful is the vision of a personal assistant that understands daily life and offers continuous, actionable feedback.

In practice, this leads to overstated capabilities. Models might claim to process 10,000+ frames, but training data often caps at 256 frames per clip, leading to degraded performance on longer inputs. We've seen this in evaluations where increasing frame sampling rates tanks accuracy on tasks requiring temporal insight.

TimeScope flips the script by emphasizing three pillars of long-video understanding:.

TimeScope’s key idea is using short video clips as “needles,” and instead of just spotting the needle, it pushes models to deeply understand the whole video. We start with a long base video (e.g., a documentary, lecture, or ambient footage) and insert one or more hand-curated short video needles (5-10 seconds each) at random positions. These needles contain the key information needed to solve the task, forcing models to process the entire input without shortcuts like sparse sampling.

Figure 1: Overview of TimeScope's needle insertion process. A long base video (1 min to 8 hours) serves as the haystack, into which we splice short video needles (~5-10 seconds). Tasks require detecting, synthesizing, or analyzing content from these needles, embedded at varying depths.

We evaluate across three needle types, each targeting a different aspect of long-video comprehension:.

Industry observers note that this tests basic retrieval and understanding of a localized event. Questions are put so that sampling a relevant frame from the needle should suffice—like asking about a shorter part in a longer video.

Example:What mode of transportation is shown in the video?

Here, we embed multiple text-based needles (e.g., 2-4 short clips displaying "secret words" via on-screen text) at different points in the video. The model must identify all words and report them in chronological order, simulating tasks like extracting timestamps or key facts from dispersed scenes. This requires scanning the full timeline and understanding relative positioning.

According to recent reports, for questions focusing on motion or sequences within a short clip, single-frame sampling won't cut it—the model needs to perceive dynamics across frames. This probes whether long-context handling preserves temporal fidelity.

Example:How many times did the man swing his axe? (a) one (b) two (c) three (d) four (e) five (f) six.

With different video lengths and varying needle placements, TimeScope measures how much video a model can really handle—and shows that performance drops as the video gets longer.

It has been revealed that to kick things off, we ran TimeScope on a suite of leading vision-language models, from open-source favorites to the juggernauts like Gemini 2.5-Pro. The results underscore the benchmark’s value: even models that claim to handle long videos well still struggle with real long-video tasks. These findings reveal clear patterns—performance cliffs around certain durations, strengths in static retrieval versus weaknesses in motion analysis—and pave the way for targeted improvements in model training. For detailed results and visualizations, check out our Hugging Face Space embedded above.

Sources indicate that model size isn’t everything. Qwen 2.5-VL 3B and 7B, as well as InternVL 2.5 models at 2B, 4B, and 8B parameters, exhibit nearly indistinguishable long-video curves to their smaller counterparts. All of them plateau at roughly the same context length, showing that simply scaling parameters does not automatically grant a longer temporal horizon.

It has been revealed that gemini 2.5-Pro is in a league of its own. It is the only model that maintains strong accuracy on videos longer than one hour.

In a recent development, trade-offs across tasks matter. Qwen 2.5-VL shines in the Information-Synthesis (OCR) task—identifying and ordering dispersed text snippets—yet it falls behind on Fine-Grained Temporal Perception, where precise motion counting is required.

TimeScope demonstrates that “hour-long video understanding” is still more slogan than reality. By revealing where even state-of-the-art models stumble on temporal reasoning, information synthesis, and motion perception, the benchmark invites us to rethink how we train and evaluate multimodal systems.

We hope this benchmark helps the community make steady, measurable progress toward models that better understand video over time.

We are open-sourcing all components of TimeScope:.

Industry observers note that ask anyone selling an old chain or a broken ring what they want to know, and it's one thing: what is this worth? A small calculator can answer that in a second, but most of the ones you find online get the details wrong. They ignore troy ounces, treat 14K as 58.5% one day and 58.3% the next, or show a "value" that no buyer will ever pay.

Recent findings suggest that in this tutorial, we'll build a gold value calculator that gets those details right. It runs on plain HTML and JavaScript, updates as the user types, works with a screen reader, keeps its state in a shareable URL and pulls a live spot price through a small Node.js endpoint. The calculation lives in one pure function, so we can test it in a few lines.

Every gold calculator comes down to three inputs: how much the item weighs, how much of that weight is actually gold, and what pure gold is trading for today.

Sources indicate that purity is measured in karats, out of 24. A 14K ring is 14 parts gold and 10 parts other metals, so it's 14 ÷ 24 = 58.3% gold. You'll also see 14K stamped as "585", which is the hallmark many manufacturers use for the same alloy. For a calculator, the karat fraction is the safer default:.

It has been revealed that the second detail most tutorials miss is the unit. Gold spot prices are quoted in USD per troy ounce, which is 31.1035 grams, not the 28.35-gram ounce on a kitchen scale. Jewelers also use pennyweight (dwt), which is 1.5552 grams. If your calculator multiplies grams by a per-ounce price without converting, every result is wrong by a factor of 31.

Put together, the formula looks like this:.

For example, with gold at $2,400 per troy ounce, 10 grams of 14K gold contains 5.83 grams of pure gold, which is worth $449.85 at melt.

It has been revealed that that $449.85 is the value of the gold content alone. Refiners and buyers pay a percentage of it, because refining, assaying and handling cost money. Depending on the buyer, the item and the market, the payout can sit well below melt value.

Recent findings suggest that that gap is why good production tools separate the two numbers. A dedicated scrap jewelry gold calculator, like the one The Alloy Market offers, lets sellers estimate what their gold is worth from its weight and karat before they send anything in. Our calculator does the same job with a payout field: leave it at 100% to see melt value, or enter a buyer's rate to see a realistic offer.

Both functions take plain values and return plain values. They don't know a DOM exists, which means the same file can run in the browser, in Node.js and in your test runner.

It has been revealed that notice that we don't round inside the calculation. Rounding happens once, at display time. Rounding in the middle of a chain of multiplications is a classic way to end up a few cents off.

Industry News: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking

📅 25 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reduce Parquet file upload and download times on Hugging Face Hub by leveraging the new Xet storage layer and Apache Arrow’s Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) feature enabling more efficient and scalable data workflows.
  • TL;DR: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) is now available in PyArrow and Pandas, enabling efficient deduplication of Parquet files on content-addressable storage systems like Hugging Face's Xet storage layer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reduce Parquet file upload and download times on Hugging Face Hub by leveraging the new Xet storage layer and Apache Arrow’s Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) feature enabling more efficient and scalable data workflows.

TL;DR: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) is now available in PyArrow and Pandas, enabling efficient deduplication of Parquet files on content-addressable storage systems like Hugging Face's Xet storage layer. CDC dramatically reduces data transfer and storage costs by uploading or downloading only the changed data chunks. Enable CDC by passing the use_content_defined_chunking argument:.

Apache Parquet is a columnar storage format that is widely used in the data engineering community.

According to recent reports, as of today, Hugging Face hosts nearly 21 PB of datasets, with Parquet files alone accounting for over 4 PB of that storage. Optimizing Parquet storage is therefore a high priority. Hugging Face has introduced a new storage layer called Xet that leverages content-defined chunking to efficiently deduplicate chunks of data reducing storage costs and improving download/upload speeds.

Sources indicate that while Xet is format agnostic, Parquet's layout and column-chunk (data page) based compression can produce entirely different byte-level representations for data with minor changes, leading to suboptimal deduplication performance. To address this, the Parquet files should be written in a way that minimizes the byte-level differences between similar data, which is where content-defined chunking (CDC) comes into play.

Let's explore the performance benefits of the new Parquet CDC feature used alongside Hugging Face's Xet storage layer.

For demonstration purposes, we will use a manageable sized subset of OpenOrca dataset.

Since pyarrow>=21.0.0 we can use Hugging Face URIs in the pyarrow functions to directly read and write parquet (and other file formats) files to the Hub using the hf:// URI scheme.

We can see that the table has been uploaded entirely (total bytes == total transfer) as upcoming data because it is not known to the Xet storage layer yet. Now read it back as a pyarrow table:.

Note that all pyarrow functions that accept a file path also accept a Hugging Face URI, like pyarrow datasets, CSV functions, incremental Parquet writer or reading only the parquet metadata:.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of the content-defined chunking feature, we will try out how it performs in case of:.

While this use case sounds trivial, traditional file systems do not deduplicate files resulting in full re-upload and re-download of the data. In contrast, a system utilizing content-defined chunking can recognize that the file content is identical and avoid unnecessary data transfer.

We can see that no upcoming data has been uploaded, and the operation was instantaneous. Now let's see what happens if we upload the same file again but to a different repository:.

Sources indicate that the upload was instantaneous again since deduplication works across repositories as well. This is a key feature of the Xet storage layer, allowing efficient data sharing and collaboration. You can read more about the details and scaling challenges in the From Chunks to Blocks: Accelerating Uploads and Downloads on the Hub blog post.

First write out the original and changed tables to local parquet files to see their sizes:.

Now upload them to Hugging Face to see how much data is actually transferred:.

Industry observers note that we can see that only the new columns and the new parquet metadata placed in the file's footer were uploaded, while the original data was not transferred again. This is a huge benefit of the Xet storage layer, as it allows us to efficiently add new columns without transferring the entire dataset again.

Same applies to removing columns, as we can see below:.

To have a better understanding of what has been uploaded, we can visualize the differences between the two parquet files using the deduplication estimation tool:.

Sources indicate that adding two newly introduced columns mean that we have unseen data pages which must be transferred (highlighted in red), but the rest of the data remains unchanged (highlighted in green), so it is not transferred again. Note the small red area in the footer metadata which almost always changes as we modify the parquet file. The dedup stats show / = where smaller ratios mean higher deduplication performance.

Also visualize the difference after removing a column:.

Since we are removing entire columns we can only see changes in the footer metadata, all the other columns remain unchanged and already existing in the storage layer, so they are not transferred again.

Another common use case is changing the column types in the table e.g. to reduce the storage size or to optimize the data for specific queries. Let's change the question_length column from int64 data type to int32 and see how much data is transferred:.

Again, we can see that only the latest column and the updated parquet metadata were uploaded. Now visualize the deduplication heatmap:.

Recent findings suggest that the first red region indicates the new column that was added, while the second red region indicates the updated metadata in the footer. The rest of the data remains unchanged and is not transferred again.

We are going to append new rows by concatenating another slice of the original dataset to the table.

Now check that only the fresh rows are being uploaded since the original data is already known to the Xet storage layer:.

In a recent development, since each column gets latest data, we can see multiple red regions. This is due to the actual parquet file specification where whole columns are laid out after each other (within each row group).

In a recent development, here comes the difficult part as insertions and deletions are shifting the existing rows which lead to different columns chunks or data pages in the parquet nomenclature. Since each data page is compressed separately, even a single row insertion or deletion can lead to a completely different byte-level representation starting from the edited row(s) to the end of the parquet file.

This parquet specific problem cannot be solved by the Xet storage layer alone, the parquet file itself needs to be written in a way that minimizes the data page differences even if there are inserted or deleted rows.

Let's try to use the existing mechanism and see how it performs.

Also visualize both cases to see the differences:.

It has been revealed that we can see that the deduplication performance has dropped significantly (higher ratio), and the deduplication heatmaps show that the compressed parquet files are quite different from each other. This is due to the fact that the inserted and deleted rows have shifted the existing rows, leading to different data pages starting from the edited row(s) to the end of the parquet file.

We can solve this problem by writing parquet files with a newly introduced pyarrow feature called content-defined chunking (CDC). This feature ensures that the columns are consistently getting chunked into data pages based on their content, similarly how the Xet storage layer deduplicates data but applied to the logical values of the columns before any serialization or compression happens.

The feature can be enabled by passing use_content_defined_chunking=True to the write_parquet function:.

Pandas also supports the latest feature:.

Let's visualize the deduplication difference before and after using the Parquet CDC feature:.

Looks much better! Since the proof of the pudding is in the eating, let's actually upload the tables using the content-defined chunking parquet feature and see how much data is transferred.

Note that we need to upload the original table first with content-defined chunking enabled:.

The uploaded data is significantly smaller than before, showing much better deduplication performance as highlighted in the heatmaps above.

Important to note that the same performance benefits apply to downloads using the huggingface_hub.hf_hub_download() and datasets.load_dataset() functions.

Industry observers note that there are cases depending on the reader/writer constraints where larger or smaller row-group sizes might be beneficial. The parquet writer implementations use fixed-sized row-groups by default, in the case of pyarrow the default is 1Mi rows. Dataset writers may change to reduce the row-group size in order to improve random access performance or to reduce the memory footprint of the reader application.

In a recent development, changing the row-group size will shift rows between row-groups, shifting values between data pages, so we have a similar problem as with inserting or deleting rows. Let's compare the deduplication performance between different row-group sizes using the parquet CDC feature:.

Datasets are often split into multiple files to improve parallelism and random access. Parquet CDC combined with the Xet storage layer can efficiently deduplicate data across multiple files even if the data is split at different boundaries.

Let's write out the dataset with three different file-level splitting then compare the deduplication performance:.

Even though we uploaded the dataset with three different sharding configurations, the overall upload size would be barely larger than the original dataset size.

So far we've used PyArrow, let’s explore using the same CDC feature with Pandas by downloading, filtering then uploading the dataset with the content-defined chunking feature enabled:.

Since Parquet CDC is applied at the parquet data page level (column chunk level), the deduplication performance depends on the filter's selectivity, or rather the distribution of the changes across the dataset. If most of the data pages are affected, then the deduplication ratio will drop significantly.

More details about the feature can be found at:.

According to recent reports, we explored the performance benefits of the new Parquet content-defined chunking feature used alongside Hugging Face's Xet storage layer. We demonstrated how it can efficiently deduplicate data in various scenarios making parquet operations faster and more storage-efficient. Comparing to traditional cloud storage solutions, the Xet storage layer with Parquet CDC can significantly reduce data transfer times and costs.

Migrate your Hugging Face repositories from Git LFS to Xet to benefit from this here: https://huggingface.co/join/xet.

We are glad to announce a long-awaited quality-of-life improvement: the Hugging Face CLI has been officially renamed from huggingface-cli to hf!

Typing huggingface-cli constantly gets old fast. More importantly, the CLI’s command structure became messy as newly introduced features were added over time (upload, download, cache management, repo management, etc.). Renaming the CLI is a chance to reorganize commands into a clearer, more consistent format.

We decided not to reinvent the wheel and instead follow a well-known CLI pattern: hf . This predictable grammar makes the Hugging Face CLI more ergonomic and discoverable, while also setting the stage for upcoming features.

To start playing with the new CLI, you’ll need to install the latest huggingface_hub version:.

and reload your terminal session. To test the install completed successfully, run hf version:.

Next, let’s explore the latest syntax with hf --help:.

According to recent reports, as we can see, commands are grouped by "resource" (hf auth, hf cache, hf repo, etc.). We also surface hf upload and hf downloadat the root level since they’re expected to be the most-used commands.

To dive deeper into any command group, simply append --help:.

Recent findings suggest that if you are used to huggingface-cli, most commands will look familiar. The biggest change affects authentication:.

All auth commands have been grouped together with the existing hf auth switch (to switch between different local profiles) and hf auth list (to list local profiles).

It has been revealed that the legacy huggingface-cli remains active and fully-functional. We’re keeping it around to ease the transition. If you use any command from the legacy CLI, you’ll see a warning that points you to the latest CLI equivalent:.

We couldn’t resist shipping our first dedicated command: hf jobs.

Hugging Face Jobs is a newly introduced service that lets you run any script or Docker image on Hugging Face Infrastructure using the hardware flavor of your choice. Billing is "pay-as-you-go", meaning you pay only for the seconds you use. Here’s how to launch your first command:.

The CLI is heavily inspired by Docker’s familiar commands:.

Learn more about Jobs by reading the guide.

According to recent reports, hugging Face Jobs are available only to Pro users and Team or Enterprise organizations. Upgrade your strategy to get started!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that TL;DR: Trackio is a newly introduced, open-source, and free experiment tracking Python library that provides a local dashboard and seamless integration with Hugging Face Spaces for easy sharing and collaboration. Since trackio is a drop-in replacement for wandb, you can get started with the syntax you already know!

If you have trained your own machine learning model, you know how crucial it is to be able to track metrics, parameters, and hyperparameters during training and visualize them afterwards to better understand your training run.

Most machine learning researchers use specific experiment tracking libraries to do this. However, these libraries can be paid, require complex setup, or lack the flexibility needed for rapid experimentation and sharing.

At Hugging Face, our science team has started using Trackio for our research projects, and we've found several key advantages over other tracking solutions:.

It has been revealed that easy Sharing and Embedding: Trackio makes it incredibly simple to share training progress with colleagues or embed plots directly in blog posts and documentation using iframes. This is especially valuable when you want to showcase specific training curves or metrics without requiring others to set up accounts or navigate complex dashboards.

Standardization and Transparency: Metrics like GPU energy usage are important to track and share with the community so we can have a better idea of the energy demands and environmental impacts of model training. Using Trackio, which directly gets information from the nvidia-smi command, makes it easy to quantify and compare energy usage and to add it to model cards.

According to recent reports, data Accessibility: Unlike some tracking tools that lock your data behind proprietary APIs, Trackio makes it straightforward to extract and analyze the data being recorded. This is crucial for researchers who need to perform custom analysis or integrate training metrics into their research workflows.

It has been revealed that flexibility for Experimentation: Trackio's lightweight design allows us to easily experiment with fresh tracking features during training runs. For instance, we can decide when to move tensors from GPU to CPU when logging tensors while training, which significantly improves training throughput when you need to track model/intermediate states without impacting performance.

According to recent reports, ok then, so what is Trackio and how do you use it? Trackio is an open-source Python library that lets you track any metrics and visualize them using a local Gradio dashboard. You can also sync this dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, which means you can then share the dashboard with other users simply by sharing a URL. Since Spaces can be private or public, this means you can share a dashboard publicly or just within members of your Hugging Face organization.

You can install trackio using pip:.

In a recent development, trackio is designed to be a drop-in replacement for experiment tracking libraries like wandb. The API is compatible with wandb.init, wandb.log, and wandb.finish, so you can simply import trackio as wandb in your code.

According to recent reports, after logging your experiments, you can launch the dashboard to visualize your results. Run the following command in your terminal:.

You can also specify a project name:.

To sync your local dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, simply pass a space_id to init:.

If you are hosting your dashboard on Spaces, you can simply share the URL or embed it anywhere using an iframe:.

Since Spaces can be private or public, this means you can share a dashboard publicly or just within members of your Hugging Face organization — all for free!

In a recent development, when you sync your Trackio dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, the data is logged to an ephemeral Sqlite database on Spaces. Because this database is reset if your Space restarts, Trackio also converts the Sqlite database to a Parquet dataset and backs it up to a Hugging Face Dataset every 5 minutes. This means you can visualize your logged metrics in a Hugging Face dataset at any time easily:.

Tip: you can set the name of this dataset by passing in a dataset_id to trackio.init().

Trackio integrates natively with Hugging Face libraries like transformers and accelerate, so you can log metrics with minimal setup.

No extra setup needed—just plug it in and start tracking.

Trackio is intentionally lightweight and is at the moment in beta. Some features found in other tracking tools, such as artifact management, or complex visualizations, are not available yet. If you'd like to have these features, please create issues here: https://github.com/gradio-app/trackio/issues.

Given Trackio's lightweight and open-source nature, we'd love to work with the machine learning community to design an experiment tracking product that works for all of us!

Please let us know any features you'd like to see in Trackio here: https://github.com/gradio-app/trackio/problems.

Many existing solutions are powerful, but they often come with setup overhead or limitations that can slow down rapid experimentation. A lightweight approach from Hugging Face feels like the right balance between functionality and ease of use... 👏.

In a recent development, what stands out most is the focus on flexibility and accessibility... 💡 Researchers, students, and independent developers often need a tool that works immediately without requiring extensive configuration or expensive subscriptions. Being able to swiftly log results, compare runs, and visualize training progress can make a huge difference when iterating on models and testing upcoming ideas. Simplicity is often underrated, especially when experimentation speed matters... ⚡🔬.

What Breaks When a Self-Hosted LLM Gateway Hits 1,000 Concurrent Streams

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • It has been revealed that we sent 1,000 streaming calls at the same moment through three self-hosted LLM gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore.
  • Langfuse's failures came from Linux's open-file limit, which Docker sets to 1,024 by default.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

It has been revealed that we sent 1,000 streaming calls at the same moment through three self-hosted LLM gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each gateway was limited to 2 CPUs. As shipped, Langfuse finished 261 of the 1,000 streams and LiteLLM finished 403. Neither failure came from the gateway's own code.

Langfuse's failures came from Linux's open-file limit, which Docker sets to 1,024 by default. LiteLLM had that problem too, plus a second one: an empty key cache sent hundreds of database lookups at once, and the ones that waited longer than 10 seconds were rejected. This article shows how each failure looked, how we traced it to its cause, and the settings that fixed it.

This benchmark measured the resource consumption of three LLM gateways under scaling concurrent streaming loads.

Full latency, memory, and feature results are available in the Langfuse vs LiteLLM vs AcruxCore benchmark.

First-token times are medians of the streams that succeeded. Up to 250 streams, every gateway succeeded. Then the errors started, and they did not look alike:.

Recent findings suggest that A 502 and a 503 point at different layers, so we expected two different causes. Two of the three turned out to share one cause.

Linux counts every network connection as an open file, and it caps how many open files one process may hold. The cap has two values. The soft limit is the cap that is in force now. The hard limit is the ceiling: a process may raise its own soft limit up to that value, and no further.

Recent findings suggest that A streaming gateway holds two connections for each stream: one from the client, and one to the model provider. That makes about 1,000 open files at 500 streams, and about 2,000 at 1,000 streams. A gateway also needs a few more files for its database, its logs and its own libraries.

In a recent development, docker on our machine gave every container a soft limit of 1,024 and a hard limit of 524,288. All three gateways received the same two numbers. What differed was how each program treats them when it starts:.

Node.js raises its own soft limit to the hard limit at startup. The Rust and Python services keep 1,024, and neither project's Compose file sets a higher value. So the two gateways ran out of open files near 500 streams, which is the point where the errors started.

Sources indicate that the out-of-files error appeared as a failed connection, not as a clear message. The Langfuse gateway's logs revealed failed connections to OpenAI, and also failed connections to Langfuse's own web service, which the gateway asks to check each key. Both come from one cause: a process that cannot open another file cannot open another socket. Its client then receives a 502.

In a recent development, read the limit the process actually has, not the one you think Docker gave it. Process 1 is usually the main process in a container:.

Recent findings suggest that if the gateway runs under a supervisor or several workers, check each worker's process ID instead of process 1. To see how close a process is to its limit under load, count its open file descriptors:.

Sources indicate that raise the limit for the gateway service in its Compose file. We used 65,536 for all three gateways:.

The same ulimits block works on the LiteLLM service. On Kubernetes or another platform, check /proc//limits inside a running container rather than assuming a value.

According to recent reports, with the open-file limit raised, the Langfuse gateway finished all 1,000 streams. LiteLLM still returned 503 errors. To separate the two causes, we ran LiteLLM with one worker and only the open-file limit raised. All 500 streams succeeded in that ladder, but 595 of 1,000 failed with 503.

In a recent development, the 503 message names the authentication database, so we read LiteLLM's logs and its source. The log gave the same reason for all 840 failed streams in these runs, 595 in that ladder and 245 in the cold-cache runs below:.

Three settings in LiteLLM explain it:.

When 500 calls arrive while the key is not in the cache, each call looks the key up in Postgres. All of those lookups queue for 10 connections. The worker was also using its whole CPU allowance at this point, which slows every query it sends and receives. We infer that this CPU load lengthens the queue, but we did not measure it separately. Whatever the share of each, the lookups at the back of the queue miss the 10-second deadline.

Industry observers note that if that explanation is right, the failures should depend on whether the key is already in the cache. So we ran 500 streams four more times. Three runs started after 75 seconds with no calls, which is longer than the 60-second cache. One run started right after a single warm-up call:.

In a recent development, the warm run had no failures. The cold runs failed by different amounts, 161, 84 and 0, because the result depends on how many lookups miss the deadline, and that changes from run to run. This probably explains why the earlier ladder succeeded at 500 and failed at 1,000. A run is a race between the lookup queue and the deadline, so a single ladder does not show where the limit is.

In a recent development, the warm-up result is the one we measured. Send one call with each virtual key after LiteLLM starts, and avoid quiet periods longer than 60 seconds before a traffic spike. A steady flow of traffic keeps the key in the cache.

It has been revealed that liteLLM also exposes three settings that act on this path. We did not test them, so treat them as places to look rather than proven fixes:.

We raised the open-file limit to 65,536 for all three gateways and gave LiteLLM 2 workers, one per CPU, as its production guide recommends for a single machine. Then we ran the full ladder again:.

It has been revealed that the open-file errors were gone for every gateway, and the Langfuse gateway gave the fastest first token of the three. LiteLLM still returned 120 × 503 at 500. That level started about 60 seconds after the first call of the ladder, so the cached key had probably just expired. All 1,000 succeeded at the next level, which started within 60 seconds of the 500 level.

Once nothing failed, CPU decided the first-token times. LiteLLM used its whole 2-CPU allowance from 100 streams on, and its median first token took 19.2 seconds at 1,000 streams. AcruxCore also used both CPUs from 100 streams on, and its first token at 1,000 streams was 3.8 s at the median and 9.7 s at p95. The Langfuse gateway peaked at 1.65 CPUs and 168 MiB, with a first token of 1.7 s at the median and 9.6 s at p95.

Each gateway also needs the rest of its stack, and that stack uses CPU too. While the Langfuse gateway served 500 streams, its whole stack used up to 3.1 CPUs, because the web service checked keys and the worker and ClickHouse stored usage. AcruxCore's whole stack peaked at 4.0 CPUs, because its API writes a trace for every call to Postgres. Size the stack around the gateway, not only the gateway container.

📚 3LM: A Benchmark for Arabic LLMs in STEM and Code

📅 01 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 📄 Paper on arXiv | 📦 Datasets on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub.
  • Industry observers note that arabic Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen notable progress in recent years, yet existing benchmarks fall short when it comes to evaluating performance in high-value technical domains.
  • Industry observers note that to address this gap, we introduce 3LM (علم), a multi-component benchmark tailored to evaluate Arabic LLMs on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects and code generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Paper on arXiv | 📦 Datasets on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub.

Industry observers note that arabic Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen notable progress in recent years, yet existing benchmarks fall short when it comes to evaluating performance in high-value technical domains. Most evaluations to date have focused on general-purpose tasks like summarization, sentiment analysis, or generic question answering. However, scientific reasoning and programming are essential for a broad range of real-world applications, from education to technical problem-solving.

Industry observers note that to address this gap, we introduce 3LM (علم), a multi-component benchmark tailored to evaluate Arabic LLMs on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects and code generation. 3LM is the first benchmark of its kind, designed specifically to test Arabic models in structured reasoning and formal logic which are domains traditionally underrepresented in Arabic NLP.

3LM is made up of three datasets, each targeting a specific evaluation axis: real-world multiple-choice STEM questions (MCQs), synthetic high-difficulty STEM questions, and translated code generation tasks.

The Native STEM benchmark consists of 865 MCQs extracted from authentic Arabic educational content, including textbooks, worksheets, and exam banks for grades 8 through 12. Questions span five core subjects: Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, and Geography.

Each question is annotated with metadata including domain and difficulty (on a 1–10 scale). The data was sourced using a pipeline that combined OCR (including LaTeX math parsing via Pix2Tex), LLM-assisted question-answer extraction, and manual review. This dataset provides a realistic testbed for evaluating factual and conceptual understanding in Arabic models using real educational materials.

To introduce greater challenge and diversity, we created a synthetic subset of 1,744 MCQs using the YourBench pipeline. This component draws from Arabic textbook text, which is chunked, summarized, and used as input to an LLM-driven question generation system. The result is a curated set of questions focused on mid-to-high difficulty reasoning, including conceptual, analytical, and application-based problems.

Industry observers note that synthetic STEM provides an notable counterbalance to native MCQs by probing deeper reasoning skills and minimizing answer bias. All generated questions underwent filtering based on clarity, structure, and content validity, followed by quality assurance via manual review.

Industry observers note that the third component of 3LM targets code generation which is a growing area of LLM evaluation. We translated and adapted the widely-used HumanEval+ and MBPP+ benchmarks into Arabic, creating the first code datasets that test Arabic LLMs on natural language prompts for programming.

Recent findings suggest that we used GPT-4o for prompt translation and validated the results with a backtranslation pipeline, rejecting low-quality samples based on ROUGE-L F1 thresholds (< 0.8). Additional human filtering ensured prompt clarity and correctness. The code and test suites remain unchanged to preserve scoring fidelity. Evaluations use the EvalPlus framework for pass@1 and pass@1+ metrics.

Each dataset in 3LM went through a multi-stage development process to ensure data quality, fairness, and representativeness.

For Native STEM, we collected Arabic PDF sources and applied a dual OCR approach to recover both plain text and math formulas. Questions were extracted using LLM-based chunking and pattern recognition, followed by classification into MCQ format with randomized answer order. Final samples were reviewed by native Arabic speakers with STEM expertise to confirm answer validity and readability.

In a recent development, for Synthetic STEM, the YourBench pipeline was adapted for Arabic input. Source documents after ingestion were first summarized, chunked and then fed to a code-controlled generator for MCQ creation. We filtered out image-dependent or ambiguous content, and only retained questions within target difficulty ranges. The result is a set of clean, high-quality synthetic Arabic MCQs for STEM.

For the Code Benchmarks, our goal was to isolate language understanding while preserving code logic. Prompt translation was handled by GPT-4o with verification via reverse translation. Code and tests were untouched to allow evaluation parity with English versions. The result is a benchmark where Arabic prompts can be evaluated directly with the EvalPlus toolchain.

Sources indicate that we evaluated over 40 LLMs, including Arabic-first, multilingual, and general-purpose base and instruction-tuned models. Evaluation was performed using both multiple-choice accuracy and generative completion metrics.

Sources indicate that in the MCQ setting, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct achieved top performance across both native (71.8%) and synthetic (67.0%) STEM subsets. For completion tasks, Gemma-3-27B indicated the strongest results with 43.2% accuracy on STEM answers.

Sources indicate that in code generation, GPT-4o demonstrated best-in-class performance on both HumanEval-ar (83.5% pass@1+) and MBPP-ar (63.6% pass@1+). These results highlight strong correlation (~0.97) between Arabic and English pass@1 scores, suggesting language-specific prompt quality has a major influence on model outcomes.

We also examined robustness under distractor perturbation, revealing that instruction-tuned models are significantly more stable than their base counterparts. Prompt engineering and zero-shot design were also shown to meaningfully affect Arabic STEM performance.

We built the benchmark to be easily reproducible using standard tools:.

All scripts, configs, and evaluation pipelines are available in our GitHub repository, and can be adapted to evaluate any model compatible with HuggingFace Transformers or OpenAI APIs.

All three datasets are open-source and hosted on HuggingFace Datasets:.

If you use 3LM in your research, please cite us:.

Industry observers note that sprint estimates usually fail because development teams heavily rely on memory and assumptions instead of evidence. They assume similar tasks will take the same amount of time. Based on these half-baked assumptions, most managers plan around ideal sprint working hours. The backlog then fills with commitments that look realistic on paper but often end up delayed.

In a recent development, actual development rarely follows that plan. There are always unexpected bugs and task dependencies that consume more time than teams account for in their estimates. Even the buffer time set aside for unexpected work may not be enough. This causes tasks to take longer than expected and pushes sprint commitments behind schedule.

Developer time tracking helps teams make better estimates with historical data. It shows how long previous tasks actually took, which provides managers with an evidence-based reference when they are planning similar work.

Reviewing this data before committing to a sprint scope turns estimation from guesswork into an evidence-based process.

Historical time data offers deeper insights, depending on how you collect and analyze it. Most importantly, it explains why planned work took longer than expected.

Before sprint planning, the following records should be reviewed.

Completed task duration: Check the time spent on finished tasks. Managers should compare similar work to understand typical development effort.

Actual versus estimated hours: Management should observe and identify differences between planned and recorded hours. If there are repeated delays, to some extent, it indicates inaccurate estimates.

Sources indicate that carryover work: Review unfinished tasks from previous sprints. Determine whether poor estimates or external delays caused the spillover..

Interruptions: Measure time spent on urgent requests and production complications. These activities reduce the development capacity that you had planned earlier.

Meetings and ceremonies: Review the time being spent on planning sessions and sprint reviews.

Industry observers note that bug-fix time: Examine hours spent resolving defects. You can also compare it to the time for developing new features.

Blocked tasks: Managers should account for the tasks delayed by missing approvals or technical dependencies.

Capacity differences: Compare team availability across sprints. Include leave and staffing changes in that time as well.

These records provide the most value when reviewed together. For example, a task may finish three days late even if the development work stayed within its estimated hours. The actual problem could be an external dependency.

Teams should understand these differences before using historical data to estimate future work.

According to recent reports, historical records provide a useful starting point for estimating fresh tasks. However, teams must interpret the data rather than simply copy previous estimates.

The following approaches can improve estimation accuracy.

Industry observers note that the first step is to consider completed tasks that resemble upcoming work. Managers should compare their requirements and technical complexity. Moreover, the development environment should be considered.

It has been revealed that for example, suppose a team needs to estimate a new API integration. Three previous integrations required 12, 15, and 18 hours of active work.

According to recent reports, the average is 15 hours. This gives developers a reference point for the newly introduced estimate.

However, the average doesn't tell the entire story. The new integration may involve unfamiliar authentication methods or more complicated testing.

According to recent reports, review the reasons behind differences in previous task durations. Check whether developers encountered unexpected bugs or unclear requirements.

Sources indicate that as a project manager, I'd consider these details before estimating for the next project. In my experience, they provide more context than an average alone.

According to recent reports, inaccurate estimates can happen; it doesn’t mean that there is a definite planning problem. However, repeated overruns across similar tasks may reveal an underlying problem.

Research suggests the pattern is widespread. A review of software estimation surveys reports that 60–80% of software projects encounter effort overruns, with the average overrun falling between 30% and 40%.

Start by calculating the difference between estimated and actual effort. Here is the formula for it.

Estimation variance (%) = [(Actual hours − Estimated hours) ÷ Estimated hours] × 100.

Suppose a task was estimated at 10 hours but needed 14 hours. The actual effort exceeded the estimate by 40%.

You can compare the results across similar tasks.

Sources indicate that for example, database migrations may repeatedly require more time than expected. This means that the team might be overlooking data validation or additional testing. Once the cause is clear, adjust future estimates accordingly.

According to recent reports, avoid increasing every estimate by the same percentage. Different types of work involve different risks. Teams can also break large tasks into smaller parts. This makes hidden development activities easier to identify.

The aim is to correct recurring estimation errors without unnecessarily increasing the entire sprint backlog.

Task duration doesn't always reflect the hours spent developing a feature.

Recent findings suggest that A study of developer workdays by Meyer and colleagues, which tracked 2,197 hours of activity across 20 developers, found that coding accounted for around 21% of the typical day. Collaborative work such as meetings and email took up roughly 24%.

It has been revealed that consider a developer who starts a feature on Monday and finishes it on Wednesday. The task took three days to complete. This is pretty straightforward, and the estimation could be based on it; however, the developer may have spent several hours in meetings. Other than that, urgent support requests could also have consumed additional time.

The actual development effort could be much lower than three full working days. This distinction matters during estimation.

Teams should record focused development time separately from interruptions. They should also track waiting periods caused by blocked tasks. A more appropriate approach would be to use active development hours to estimate similar future work. They should also account for recurring interruptions when calculating sprint capacity.

In a recent development, for example, a task may regularly wait for security approval. Adding more development hours to its estimate won't resolve that delay.

Instead, the team should recognize the dependency and consider its effect on delivery.

If managers are able to separate these activities, it will help create better estimates without confusing effort with elapsed time.

A precise estimate can create false confidence when a task involves substantial uncertainty.

Suppose similar tasks previously required between 12 and 20 hours. If you estimate the next task at exactly 14 hours, it will overlook crucial differences.

It has been revealed that A range of 12–20 hours provides a clearer picture of the possible effort. Developers can then discuss what might push the task toward either end of the range.

For example, the lower estimate can be directly applied to integration, and the upper estimate might be considered for unfamiliar code or additional testing.

In such scenarios, if the requirements stay unclear, consider a short technical investigation before finalizing the estimate. This can help identify dependencies and reduce uncertainty.

However, estimate ranges should still support practical planning decisions. Teams need to determine how much capacity to reserve for the work.

Choose a planning assumption that reflects the task's risk and available capacity.

As developers learn more about the task, they can refine the estimate.

Historical time data should affect how much work a team accepts during sprint planning. Better estimates offer little value if teams continue making unrealistic commitments.

Reduce Scope After Repeated Overruns.

If several sprints end with unfinished tasks, it is best that you first review why the team missed its commitments in the first place. Once you have identified the causes, use those findings to reduce the next sprint's scope.

Teams should prioritize work that supports the sprint goal. Moreover, avoid adding extra tasks just because they appear manageable during planning.

Reserve Capacity for Unplanned Work.

Sources indicate that production incidents and urgent requests can disrupt planned development. To get more reliable estimations, review how much time these activities consumed in previous sprints. Then reserve an appropriate amount of capacity.

Adjust for Complexity and Dependencies.

Recent findings suggest that historical estimates become less reliable in case unfamiliar technology or additional dependencies are involved. It is best to break complex tasks into smaller components where possible. This helps developers assess the work more accurately.

Nominal capacity represents scheduled working hours, whereas actual capacity reflects the time available after accounting for other commitments.

The Scrum Guide identifies previous performance and upcoming capacity as notable inputs to sprint forecasting.

In a recent development, when you are selecting backlog items, consider both. Additionally, avoid committing every available hour or deducting the same interruption twice.

According to recent reports, historical time data is useful for sprint planning. Most development teams already use project management tools that include basic time tracking features.

Industry observers note that however, these tools don't always break down how developers spend their working hours. For clearer time data, a feature-specific time tracker is more useful because it provides more details about tasks and workloads.

TimeBee is one such developer time tracking tool I've used. It tracks working hours and time spent on projects and tasks. It also provides attendance records and workforce activity reports.

With this data, teams can review how much time previous tasks required. For example, developers can record hours spent building a feature. They can also track debugging and revisions separately. Later, managers can compare these records with the original estimates. This helps them plan similar work more accurately.

TimeBee also tracks website and application activity. These reports can help teams understand how working hours are distributed.

However, not all activities reflect actual development effort. Sometimes a developer just spends time reviewing documentation or discussing technical problems. Such work may not always appear in TimeBee as active computer use.

In a recent development, apart from that, attendance, leave, and overtime records from TimeBee can help managers calculate sprint capacity. They can review developer availability before deciding how much work to include in the next sprint.

In a recent development, one thing to remember is that developer time tracking should help teams understand workload patterns. It shouldn't be used to monitor every minute of a developer's day. Management should be careful that the aim is to improve estimates and make more realistic sprint commitments.

Sprint retrospectives should include a review of how the planning is going. If you have made a plan, it doesn’t mean you cannot make changes to it. During sprints, keep comparing original estimates with actual task hours. Track your unfinished work for recurring delays.

Ask developers what caused significant differences. Some tasks may have required additional testing. Others may have been delayed by dependencies. Select one specific improvement for the next sprint.

Not every estimation difference indicates a planning failure. Unexpected technical challenges are part of software development.

The objective is to improve forecasts over time rather than eliminate every variance.

It has been revealed that historical time data provides a more stable foundation for sprint planning. Developer time tracking helps teams understand what is actually happening within the sprint rather than creating unnecessary pressure for them.

Other than that, the data also reveals how interruptions affect available development hours.

However, time data should guide planning rather than dictate it.

Industry observers note that 1. What is the difference between sprint velocity and time-based capacity planning?

According to recent reports, sprint velocity measures how much work a team has completed during a sprint. It is usually measured in story points. Contrary to this, time-based capacity planning calculates the hours available for planned work. It accounts for meetings and other responsibilities.

Velocity helps predict future delivery based on past performance. Capacity planning indicates whether the team has enough time to meet its commitments.

Recent findings suggest that 2. Which time tracking metrics are most useful for improving Agile sprint forecasts? The most useful metrics include estimated versus actual hours, task completion time, and unplanned work.

According to recent reports, bug-fix time, rework, and blocked tasks also provide valuable insights. Teams should also review available capacity across previous sprints.

Recent findings suggest that these metrics help sort out recurring delays and estimation errors. They allow teams to forecast workloads more accurately and make realistic sprint commitments.

**3. How can development teams improve estimates when historical time tracking data is incomplete? **.

Sources indicate that teams can start with available task records and completed sprint backlogs. Developer feedback can help fill information gaps. Similar tasks from previous projects may also provide useful estimates.

It has been revealed that when data is limited, teams should use estimate ranges instead of fixed hours. Consistent time tracking in future sprints will gradually provide more reliable planning data.

4. How can time tracking data help balance workloads across developers during sprint planning?

Time tracking data shows how much time developers spend on assigned tasks and other responsibilities. Managers can review these records to identify uneven workloads. They can then distribute upcoming tasks based on available capacity.

Technical expertise and task complexity should also influence assignments. This helps prevent over commitment and supports a more balanced workload across the development team.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GPT OSS is a hugely anticipated open-weights release by OpenAI, designed for powerful reasoning, agentic tasks, and versatile developer use cases. It comprises two models: a big one with 117B parameters (gpt-oss-120b), and a smaller one with 21B parameters (gpt-oss-20b). Both are mixture-of-experts (MoEs) and use a 4-bit quantization scheme (MXFP4), enabling fast inference (thanks to fewer active parameters, see details below) while keeping resource usage low. The large model fits on a single H100 GPU, while the small one runs within 16GB of memory and is perfect for consumer hardware and on-device applications.

To make it even better and more impactful for the community, the models are licensed under the Apache 2.0 license, along with a minimal usage policy:.

According to recent reports, we aim for our tools to be used safely, responsibly, and democratically, while maximizing your control over how you use them. By using gpt-oss, you agree to comply with all applicable law.

According to OpenAI, this release is a meaningful step in their commitment to the open-source ecosystem, in line with their stated mission to make the benefits of AI broadly accessible. Many use cases rely on private and/or local deployments, and we at Hugging Face are super excited to welcome OpenAI to the community. We believe these will be long-lived, inspiring and impactful models.

OpenAI GPT OSS models are accessible through Hugging Face’s Inference Providers service, allowing you to send requests to any supported provider using the same JavaScript or Python code. This is the same infrastructure that powers OpenAI’s official demo on gpt-oss.com, and you can use it for your own projects.

Recent findings suggest that below is an example that uses Python and the super-fast Cerebras provider. For more info and additional snippets, check the inference providers section in the model cards and the dedicated guide we crafted for these models.

Inference Providers also implements an OpenAI-compatible Responses API, the most advanced OpenAI interface for chat models, designed for more flexible and intuitive interactions.Below is an example using the Responses API with the Fireworks AI provider. For more details, check out the open-source responses.js project.

You need to install the latest transformers release (v4.55.1 or later), as well as accelerate and kernels. We also recommend installing triton 3.4 or better, as it unblocks support for mxfp4 quantization on CUDA hardware:.

The model weights are quantized in mxfp4 format, which was originally available on GPUs of the Hopper or Blackwell families, but now works on previous CUDA architectures (including Ada, Ampere, and Tesla). Installing triton 3.4, together with the kernels library, makes it possible to download optimized mxfp4 kernels on first use, achieving large memory savings. With these components in place, you can run the 20B model on GPUs with 16 GB of RAM. This includes many consumer cards (3090, 4090, 5080) as well as Colab and Kaggle!

If the previous libraries are not installed (or you don’t have a compatible GPU), loading the model will fall back to bfloat16, unpacked from the quantized weights.

The following snippet shows simple inference with the 20B model. As explained, it runs on 16 GB GPUs when using mxfp4, or ~48 GB in bfloat16.

We have packaged and integrated their optimized kernel in kernels-community/vllm-flash-attn3. At the time of writing, this super-fast kernel has been tested on Hopper cards with PyTorch 2.7 and 2.8. We expect increased coverage in the coming days. We recommend you use mxfp4 if your GPU supports it. If you can additionally use Flash Attention 3, then by all means do enable it!

It has been revealed that GPT OSS models are reasoning models: they therefore require a very large generation size (maximum number of latest tokens) for evaluations, as their generation will first contain reasoning, then the actual answer. Using too small a generation size risks interrupting the prediction in the middle of reasoning, which will cause false negatives. The reasoning trace should then be removed from the model answer before computing metrics, to avoid parsing errors, especially with math or instruct evaluations.

Here’s an example on how to evaluate the models with lighteval (you need to install from source).

For the 20B model, this should give you 69.5 (+/-1.9) for IFEval (strict prompt), and 63.3 (+/-8.9) for AIME25 (in pass@1), scores within expected range for a reasoning model of this size.

If you want to do your custom evaluation script, note that to filter out the reasoning tags properly, you will need to use skip_special_tokens=False in the tokenizer, in order to get the full trace in the model output (to filter reasoning using the same string pairs as in the example above) - you can discover why below.

OpenAI GPT OSS uses the concept of “channels” in its outputs. Most of the time, you will see an “analysis” channel that contains things that are not intended to be sent to the end-user, like chains of thought, and a “final” channel containing messages that are actually intended to be displayed to the user.

Assuming no tools are being used, the structure of the model output looks like this:.

Most of the time, you should ignore everything except the text after <|channel|>final<|message|>. Only this text should be appended to the chat as the assistant message, or displayed to the user. There are two exceptions to this rule, though: You may need to include analysis messages in the history during training or if the model is calling external tools.

Industry observers note that when training: If you’re formatting examples for training, you generally want to include the chain of thought in the final message. The right place to do this is in the thinking key.

You can feel free to include thinking keys in previous turns, or when you’re doing inference rather than training, but they will generally be ignored. The chat template will only ever include the most recent chain of thought, and only in training (when add_generation_prompt=False and the final turn is an assistant turn).

It has been revealed that the reason why we do it this way is subtle: The OpenAI gpt-oss models were trained on multi-turn data where all but the final chain of thought was dropped. This means that when you want to fine-tune an OpenAI gpt-oss model, you should do the same.

OpenAI GPT OSS is unusual because it distinguishes between a “system” message and a “developer” message at the start of the chat, but most other models only use “system”. In GPT OSS, the system message follows a strict format and contains information like the current date, the model identity and the level of reasoning effort to use, and the “developer” message is more freeform, which makes it (very confusingly) similar to the “system” messages of most other models.

Sources indicate that to make GPT OSS easier to use with the standard API, the chat template will treat a message with “system” or “developer” role as the developer message. If you want to modify the actual system message, you can pass the specific arguments model_identity or reasoning_effort to the chat template:.

To pass custom tools, you can pass them either as JSON schema or as Python functions with type hints and docstrings using the tools argument. See the chat template tools documentation for more details, or you can just modify the example below:.

Tech Report: AI-powered robot learns how to harvest tomatoes more efficiently

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that farm labor shortages are pushing agriculture toward greater automation, especially when it comes to harvesting.
  • To tackle this challenge, Assistant Professor Takuya Fujinaga of Osaka Metropolitan University's Graduate School of Engineering developed a system that trains robots to assess how easy each tomato is to harvest before attempting to pick it.
  • His approach combines image recognition with statistical analysis to determine the best angle for picking each fruit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that farm labor shortages are pushing agriculture toward greater automation, especially when it comes to harvesting. But not all crops are easy for machines to handle. Tomatoes, for example, grow in clusters, which means a robot must carefully select ripe fruit while leaving unripe ones untouched. This requires precise control and smart decision-making.

To tackle this challenge, Assistant Professor Takuya Fujinaga of Osaka Metropolitan University's Graduate School of Engineering developed a system that trains robots to assess how easy each tomato is to harvest before attempting to pick it.

His approach combines image recognition with statistical analysis to determine the best angle for picking each fruit. The robot analyzes visual details such as the tomato itself, its stems, and whether it is hidden behind leaves or other parts of the plant. These inputs guide the robot in choosing the most effective way to approach and pick the fruit.

From Detection to "Harvest-Ease" Decision-Making.

It has been revealed that this method shifts away from traditional systems that focus only on detecting and identifying fruit. Instead, Fujinaga introduces what he calls "harvest-ease estimation." "This moves beyond simply asking 'can a robot pick a tomato?' to thinking about 'how likely is a successful pick?', which is more meaningful for real-world farming," he explained.

In testing, the system achieved an 81% success rate, exceeding expectations. About one-quarter of the successful picks came from tomatoes that were harvested from the side after an initial front-facing attempt failed. This indicates the robot can adjust its approach when the first attempt is not successful.

The research underscores how many variables affect robotic harvesting, including how tomatoes cluster, the shape and position of stems, surrounding leaves, and visual obstruction. "This research establishes 'ease of harvesting' as a quantitatively evaluable metric, bringing us one step closer to the realization of agricultural robots that can make informed decisions and act intelligently," Fujinaga said.

Future of Human-Robot Collaboration in Farming.

Looking ahead, Fujinaga envisions robots that can independently judge when crops are ready to be picked. "This is expected to usher in a upcoming form of agriculture where robots and humans collaborate," he explained. "Robots will automatically harvest tomatoes that are easy to pick, while humans will handle the more challenging fruits.".

The findings were published in Smart Agricultural Technology.
